parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a company to book a guided walking holiday for himself and his wife.
script: Good morning, Wayfarer Walking Holidays, Maeve speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, good morning. I'd like to book a guided walking holiday for my wife and me, please. We picked up your brochure at a travel fair last month.
Lovely. Let me take a few details first. Could I have your surname, please?
Thank you, Mr Whitcombe. And a contact number?
My mobile's the best one. It's 07700 914 382.
07700 914 382. Got that. Now, which holiday were you interested in? We have the Cornish Coast Path, the Highland Trail and the Ullmoor Way.
Well, my wife was keen on the Highland Trail, but the photographs of the Ullmoor Way won us over in the end. That's the one through the hills and valleys, isn't it?
That's right, seven days from village to village. When were you hoping to start?
Let me see. Oh, I'm afraid the 7th is full. We do have a group leaving on 14 June, though, and there are still a few places.
The 14th would be fine, actually. It's better for us. Our daughter has her graduation on the 8th, so we'd have had to rush away.

Wonderful, I'll put you down for 14 June. Now, about accommodation. Most nights are in small country hotels, but on the middle nights you can choose between the Crown Hotel in the village of Aldersey or a farmhouse bed and breakfast.
Oh, the hotel, I think. My wife does like a proper bath after a long walk.
Ah, the thing is, the Crown is completely booked that week. There's a wedding.
Never mind. The farmhouse it is, then. I'm sure it'll be charming.
It is, and the breakfasts are famous. Speaking of food, does anyone in your party have any dietary requirements?
I eat anything, but my wife is vegetarian. And she's allergic to nuts, no, sorry, that's our daughter. My wife's allergy is to shellfish. Will that be a problem?

Not at all. I'll make a note of vegetarian and a shellfish allergy, and the hosts will be told. Now, our luggage transfer service is optional. The company van carries your main bags from place to place, so you only have to walk with a small day pack.
That sounds sensible. How much is it?
Normally it's 40 pounds per person for the week, but because you're booking more than two months ahead, you get a discount, so it comes to 35 pounds.
Good, we'll take it. Right, what about the walking itself?
The walks are graded easy, moderate or challenging. The challenging grade means up to eight hours a day on rough ground.
My wife would love that, but I've got a bad knee, so it'd have to be the easy one for me. Though I suppose she'd be bored.
Most couples choose the middle grade, moderate. The days are around five hours, and there's a shorter option on the fourth day if anyone is tired.
Then moderate it is. How do we get to the start?
The first night is in Harrowgate. Some people drive, but the car park at the start is tiny, so most travel by train to Harrowgate station and our guide collects them at 10 o'clock.
Train it is, then. That's much less stress.
Perfect. Finally, we ask for a deposit of 100 pounds per person to secure your places. Would you like to pay now?
Yes, I'll put a cheque in the post this afternoon.
I'm so sorry, we stopped accepting cheques last year. You can pay by credit card over the phone, or send a bank transfer.
Oh, I see. I don't like giving card details over the phone, so I'll do the bank transfer when we finish this call. Could you email me the details?
Of course. I'll send the confirmation and the bank details straight away. Thank you for choosing Wayfarer, Mr Whitcombe, and enjoy the Ullmoor Way.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The manager of a leisure centre announces changes that will happen while a new fitness suite is built.
script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming along. I'm Dale Prentice, the manager here at Castlegate Leisure Centre, and I'd like to take a few minutes to explain what is going to change over the next few months. I know a lot of you have been asking, so I'll try to cover everything, and there will be a leaflet at reception for you to take home afterwards.

First, the big news. As you will have seen from the notices, we are building a new fitness suite. The original plan was to put it on the west side of the building, but the architects found that the ground there is too soft. So it will go on the east side, where the old tennis courts used to be. The courts have been closed for a year anyway, so nobody loses out.

Now, when will it be ready? The builders move in on 3 February. The first estimate was that they would finish by the end of March, but they now tell me the end of April is more realistic, because the steel for the roof is arriving late. I've worked in this job long enough to know that building work rarely runs to time, so please do not book your birthday party for April just yet. We will put the exact opening date on our website as soon as we have it.

Next, how you get in. During the work, the main entrance on Castle Street will be closed, because the lorries need it. Please use the temporary entrance on Fenwick Road. That's F-E-N-W-I-C-K Road, round at the back, next to the recycling bins. There will be signs, and staff in yellow jackets will be there in the mornings to point you in the right direction.

Many of you have asked about the gym. It will stay open throughout, but in a smaller space, so it will get busy. To help with that, we are going to open at 6.30 each morning instead of 7 o'clock. Some people suggested opening at 6, but we simply cannot staff it that early. Parking is the other big worry. Half of our car park will be fenced off. So we've agreed a deal with the council. Members can use the Station Road car park free of charge for up to 3 hours, if you get your ticket stamped at reception. Usually, the limit there is 2 hours, so this is a real help.

Let me now go through the facilities one at a time, because the effect is different for each. The swimming pool stays open, but only the small teaching pool. The main pool needs a new filter while we have the builders here, so it will be empty for most of the period. Lane swimmers, I'm afraid you will have to share the small pool, and I'd suggest you come in the middle of the day, when it's quietest.

The café, which as you know is currently next to the pool, will move to the foyer of the sports hall. It will serve the same menu, with the same people behind the counter, so you will still be able to get your usual coffee and cake. It will just be in a different place.

The climbing wall, I'm sorry to say, will be closed for the whole time. It shares a wall with the building site, and the engineers say the vibration is too much. I know that's a disappointment for the regulars. We will keep your memberships going without charge for those weeks, and I'll tell you the details at the desk.

The soft play area for the little ones will stay open. However, it will close at 4 in the afternoon instead of 6, because we are short of staff for the evening supervision during the works. I realise that's awkward for parents who finish work late, and we are looking at whether Saturday mornings could be extended to make up for it.

Finally, the lockers. These normally cost a pound coin each time, but the changing rooms will be smaller and we don't want queues of people searching for change. So they will be free of charge until the work is done. Please make sure you take your belongings with you when you leave.

One more thing. Membership prices will not change this year, and nobody will lose their place in any course. If you have any questions, please come and find me or leave a note at reception, and I will answer every one personally. Thank you very much for your patience, and I promise it will be worth the wait.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two architecture students discuss the model of a low-cost house that they are building for a course project.
script: Okay, Cal, the model is due in two weeks, so we need to decide what we're doing about the first version.
Yeah. I looked at the photos again last night. The outside looks fine, but you can't really see how the rooms fit together. Everything's hidden under the roof.
True. I thought the real problem was that it was so fragile. It nearly fell apart when we carried it to the studio.
That too, but the tutor's main comment was about the inside. She wants the assessors to be able to see the layout without taking it to pieces.
So a roof that lifts off.
Exactly. And the walls on one side could be lower, so people can look in.
Fine. And I'm still happy with one storey. Remember we thought about two?

Yes. A second floor would have given us more space on a small plot. I thought the planning rules might stop us, but it turns out they'd allow two storeys. It's the cost. The brief says the house must be built for under 40,000 pounds, and a second floor needs a much stronger frame and a staircase. That's where the money goes.
Right. And with one storey, we can use an open-plan living area, which saves on internal walls too.
Good. What about the solar panels? Should we put them on the roof of the model?
Well, they'd push the cost over the limit. The panels alone are about 4,000.
But they'd pay for themselves in a few years. I'd hate to leave them out altogether.
I think we should show them, but mark them clearly as an optional extra, with the price listed separately. That way the main cost stays under the limit and we still show we've thought about energy.
That's smart. I'll do a little label for them.
Now, the cost breakdown. You wanted to hand out a spreadsheet, didn't you?
I did, but it'd be forty lines long. And a pie chart wouldn't show the actual figures.
Exactly. What about a simple table, just walls, roof, windows, floor and so on, on a poster next to the model? People can read it while they look at the house.
Okay, that works. We can keep the full spreadsheet in case anybody asks.
One more thing. I want to ask Dr Hale whether we can assume the walls are built with recycled bricks. It would cut the cost by about 15 per cent, but the supplier isn't on the approved list.
Good idea. Better to ask than to find out on the day. Would she agree to a longer deadline, do you think?
I doubt it, so let's not ask for that. Right, materials for the model. Last time we used card for the walls and they bent.
I'd go for balsa wood for the walls. It's strong and easy to cut.

It's expensive though, and we need a lot. Foam board is cheaper and stays flat. I'd save the balsa for the roof, because that has to be light enough to lift off, and the balsa will give it a good edge.
Fair enough. Foam board for the walls, balsa for the roof. And windows? Last time we just drew them on.
I found some clear plastic from old packaging. We can cut it to size and glue it behind the frames. Glass would look nice, but it's far too dangerous to cut.
Plastic is fine. What about the garden? I was going to use sand for the path.
Sand gets everywhere. The workshop has some fine gravel left over from another project. That would look more realistic.
Great. And trees? I'd thought about cloth, but it doesn't hold its shape.
Twisted wire, then. There's a whole box of it in the workshop, and we can cover the ends with green sponge.
Perfect. I'll make a list and we can start cutting tomorrow.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about noise pollution and its effects on health.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that we all live with every day but rarely think of as a health issue: noise. When we talk about pollution, we usually think of smoke, chemicals, or rubbish. But sound, if it is loud enough or constant enough, is a pollutant too, and in recent years researchers have been paying it much more attention.

Let me begin with the basics. We measure the loudness of sound in units called decibels. A quiet library is about 30 decibels. Ordinary conversation is around 60. A busy road or a food blender is nearer 85. Now, many people believe that hearing damage only begins at 100 decibels, which is the level of a rock concert. In fact, long exposure to anything above 85 decibels, say eight hours a day for years, can damage hearing permanently. So the factory worker or the farmer on a noisy tractor is at risk, not just the music fan.

But hearing loss is only part of the story. What is more surprising, and what has driven most of the research in the last twenty years, is the effect of noise on the rest of the body. One large study in Europe looked at people who lived under the flight path of a major airport. Compared with people in quieter areas, they were much more likely to suffer from high blood pressure. That was true even after the researchers had allowed for age, smoking and income.

Why should this happen? The explanation seems to be that the body reacts to sudden noise as a threat, even when we are not conscious of it. Heart rate goes up and we produce more of what is known as the stress hormone, cortisol. That response is useful if you are escaping from a predator, but if it happens many times each night, because of passing trains or lorries, it takes a toll. This is why night noise is the most worrying. Even when people do not wake up, their sleep is lighter and less restful.

Children are affected too. A well-known study followed pupils in schools near a railway line. I had expected the problems to show up in mathematics, but in fact the children's scores fell most in reading. The researchers suggested that the noise made it hard for pupils to concentrate on the sounds of words, and when the trains were rerouted, the scores improved.

More recently, studies in several cities have linked long-term exposure to traffic noise with a higher risk of dementia in older adults. I should stress that this is a link and not proof of cause. People who live beside busy roads also breathe more polluted air, so it is hard to separate the two effects. But the pattern is consistent enough to take seriously.

So what can be done? Let me suggest a few practical measures, starting with town planning. The most common solution is to build noise barriers beside motorways and railways. Planting trees is often suggested, and people do find a green view calming, but a belt of trees reduces actual sound only by a tiny amount. Barriers are much more effective.

Then there is traffic management. Several European cities have lowered the night speed limit on main roads. Normally it is 50 kilometres per hour, but they have brought it down to 30, which cuts engine and tyre noise noticeably and also makes the roads safer. Some cities have also banned heavy lorries from residential districts between ten at night and six in the morning.

At the level of buildings, the most cost-effective step is better windows. Triple glazing helps, but the key factor is the thickness of the glass. Thicker panes block low-frequency noise from traffic much better than ordinary windows, and an older building can be improved without any major rebuilding.

Finally, there is what we can do as individuals. Because headphones sit close to the ear, they are a hidden source of risk. A good rule is to keep the volume below 60 per cent of the maximum, and to take a break from listening after an hour. Many people use 80 per cent, which is too high. If you can hear your music when you are standing next to someone, it is already too loud.

To sum up, noise is not just an annoyance. It is a real public health problem, and the good news is that many of the solutions are simple and inexpensive. In next week's session, we will look at how cities map their noise levels. Thank you.

passages.title: Recycling at Alder Court: a guide for residents
paras: All 48 flats share a bin store at the rear of the building, reached through the door beside the bicycle shed. The store is unlocked between 7 am and 9 pm. Outside these hours, please keep your rubbish in your flat. The bin store is cleaned every Friday by the building's cleaning contractor, but residents are asked to help by keeping the floor clear and closing the door behind them to keep out foxes and other animals.

Blue bins are for paper, flattened cardboard, cans and plastic bottles. Please rinse items before putting them in, but there is no need to remove labels. Plastic bags and polystyrene must not go in the blue bins, because the sorting plant cannot process them. Pizza boxes should be put in the black bin if they are greasy, as the grease spoils the paper. Newspapers, magazines and junk mail can be placed in the blue bins loose, though many residents find it easier to tie them in a bundle with string.
Glass bottles and jars go in the green bins. Remove the lids first and put them in the blue bin with the cans.

Food waste goes into the small brown caddy provided with your flat. Compostable liners are free from the caretaker, Mr Osei, whose office is by the main entrance and is open on weekday mornings. Caddies should be emptied into the large brown bin, which is collected every Tuesday. Meat, fish and cooked food may be put in the caddy, and in warm weather it is a good idea to keep it in the fridge or on a cool windowsill so that it does not smell.
Everything else goes in the black bins. The blue and green bins are collected every second Thursday, and the black bins are emptied weekly on Mondays.

Large items such as sofas and fridges cannot be left in the bin store. Residents can arrange a free collection of up to three bulky items a year by phoning the council. Old batteries and light bulbs may be left in the box in the lobby, which is emptied monthly.

If the bins are full, please do not leave bags on the floor. Contact the caretaker, who will arrange an extra collection. Repeated problems with sorting will lead to a warning letter from the management company. New residents will find a copy of this guide, together with a colour chart for the bins, in their welcome pack. Spare copies are available from the caretaker.

passages.title: Home services: trusted local firms
paras: A  Brook & Sons Plumbing. Leaking tap or blocked drain? We give a free written quote before any work begins, so you know the price in advance. We are open Monday to Saturday, 8 am to 6 pm. Every repair is covered by our 12-month guarantee: if it fails, we will fix it free of charge. Call 01632 960 411.  Our plumbers wear uniform and carry identity cards, and all work is carried out with care for your floors and furniture.

B  Greenfingers Garden Care. Lawns cut weekly or fortnightly, hedges trimmed and flower beds weeded. We bring our own tools and take away all green waste, and the cost of this is included in our price. Customers over 65 receive 10 per cent off every visit. Call 01632 960 522.  We are a family business and have looked after gardens in this part of town for over twenty years. We also offer a seasonal planting service in spring and autumn.

C  Sparkle Home Cleaning. Our friendly, fully vetted cleaners bring all their own products and equipment. Choose from a regular weekly clean or a one-off deep clean. The minimum booking is two hours. New customers pay half price for their first clean. Call 01632 960 633.  We can arrange to visit while you are at work, and you may choose a different cleaner at any time if you prefer.

D  Voltright Electricians. Registered electricians for rewiring, new sockets and lighting. Our emergency line is staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and we offer free telephone advice with no obligation. Landlords: we can give you the safety certificate you need before your property is let. Call 01632 960 744.  Our electricians arrive on time and tidy up after themselves. Appointments are available in the evenings and at weekends for the convenience of busy customers.

passages.title: Quality standards at Pennant Contact Centre
paras: Every customer who phones Pennant Contact Centre should receive the same high standard of service, whichever adviser answers the call. Our quality standards explain what this means in practice.  They also form the basis of the monthly reports that we send to our client companies, who rely on us to represent their businesses to the public.

Answering calls. The aim is for 90 per cent of calls to be answered within 20 seconds. Advisers begin every call with a greeting, their first name and the name of the client company they are speaking for. Advisers may use their own words, but the three elements must always be included.  New advisers practise the greeting during their first week of training, and team leaders listen in on live calls during the first month to offer help where it is needed.

Handling calls. There is no time limit on a call. Our measure of success is whether the customer's problem is solved first time. If an adviser cannot solve a problem during the call, they must give the customer a clear time by which to expect an answer, and they must contact the customer again within 24 hours, even if only to report progress.  This approach is sometimes difficult for new advisers, who may feel under pressure to finish quickly, but experience shows that customers prefer a full answer to a fast one, and that fewer repeat calls are made as a result.

Monitoring. Each month, four calls per adviser are chosen at random and assessed by a member of the quality team against a checklist of 20 points. Advisers are told their results within five working days, at a one-to-one meeting. A score of 85 per cent or higher is expected. Advisers whose score is lower receive coaching from their team leader. Where scores remain below standard for three consecutive months, a formal review is held.  The checklist covers the greeting, the accuracy of information given, the adviser's tone of voice and whether the call was closed politely.

Difficult calls. Advisers are not expected to accept abuse. After two warnings, an adviser may end a call, but must record the reason. Customers who ask to speak to a manager should be transferred if one is available. If not, a manager will phone the customer back on the same day.  Advisers who deal with a particularly upsetting call may take a short break afterwards, and a team leader will check that they are all right.

Customer feedback. A text message survey is sent after about one call in ten. The centre's overall score is published each month on the staff noticeboard. Staff may suggest improvements by email to the quality team, and the best idea of each quarter wins a small prize.

passages.title: Joining the Pennant staff pension scheme
paras: All employees who are 22 or older and earn more than 10,000 pounds a year are enrolled in the pension scheme automatically after their first three months of work. You do not need to complete any forms to join.

Both you and the company pay into your pension. You contribute 5 per cent of your salary and the company adds 8 per cent. Your contribution is taken from your pay before tax is calculated, which means that the real cost to you is lower than it appears on your payslip.

If you do not wish to be in the scheme, you may opt out within 30 days of being enrolled. You will need to collect an opt-out form from the Human Resources office. Any money already paid in will be returned to you.

The scheme is run by an independent group of trustees, who invest the money on your behalf. Each April you will receive a statement showing how much your pension is worth. You can take your pension from the age of 57, though the normal retirement age at Pennant is 66.  A helpline is also available to answer questions about the scheme, and an adviser from the trustees visits the office twice a year to meet employees who would like to talk in person.

If you leave the company, your pension remains invested in your name. You can leave it where it is, or you can ask for it to be moved to a scheme run by your new employer.  Part-time employees are treated in exactly the same way as full-time staff, and the pension of an employee who takes a career break is left untouched.

You can increase your pension by paying extra amounts directly from your salary. You can start, stop or change these amounts four times a year. In addition, if you die while working for the company, a lump sum equal to four times your annual salary is paid to the people you have named.

passages.title: The village that switched itself on
paras: A  In the hills of the north, where the river Kel runs fast over stones, lies the village of Kelderby. About 600 people live here, in grey stone houses, around a church, a school and a pub. It looks like many other villages, apart from the turbines turning on the ridge above it. Since 2016, Kelderby has produced more electricity than it uses, and nearly all of its buildings are heated without gas or oil. Visitors come from as far away as Japan to find out how it was done.  The school's head teacher says that her pupils now learn about renewable energy in the best classroom imaginable, which is the one outside the window.

B  The story began with a storm. In the winter of 2011, falling trees brought down the power lines, and the village was without electricity for nine days. Elderly residents were helped by neighbours, who brought hot meals and chopped firewood. At a meeting in the school hall, a retired engineer, Ruth Calloway, asked a simple question: why should a place with so much wind and water depend on a cable from somewhere else? Within a month, a group of 20 volunteers had formed the Kelderby Energy Society.  Some of the older residents remembered similar winters from their childhood, when the village had no mains electricity at all and farms relied on water wheels, but the nine days of darkness felt like a warning that the modern system was more fragile than it looked.

C  The plan they drew up had four parts. A small hydroelectric turbine was to be placed in the river beside the old mill, three wind turbines on the ridge, and solar panels on the roofs of the school and the church. Finally, a boiler burning wood chips from local forests would provide heat for the school, the community hall and 30 homes through underground pipes. None of the equipment was new to science. The challenge was to persuade a small community to pay for it.  The wood chips come from thinning work carried out on plantations within 10 miles, which means that the fuel is cut and delivered by neighbours rather than by a distant supplier, and the ash is returned to local farms as fertiliser.

D  The total cost was 1.2 million pounds. The society sold shares, with a minimum purchase of 250 pounds, and more than half of the households in the village bought at least one. Some bought on behalf of grandchildren. A regional grant covered about a quarter of the cost, and a bank lent the remainder, once it was satisfied that the villagers were serious. 'People who have invested their savings take an interest in whether the wind is blowing,' Calloway says.  Volunteers also spent evenings knocking on doors to explain the plan, and the society published its accounts openly so that anyone could check how the money was being spent.

E  Not everyone was convinced. A group of residents worried that turbines would spoil the view from the ridge, which has been walked for centuries. Others feared the noise. After months of argument, the society changed its plans. It reduced the number of turbines from five to three, moved them 600 metres further from the nearest house, and painted them a soft grey-green. A vote in the school hall approved the revised plan by a large majority, and even some of the doubters now admit the turbines have become part of the landscape.

F  The first power was sent into the system in 2014. By 2018, the village was producing about 115 per cent of the electricity it consumed over a year. The surplus is sold, and the money has been put to practical uses. A community minibus now links the village to the market town three times a day, and grants of up to 2,000 pounds help households add insulation to old stone walls. Bills for the average household have fallen by about a third.  The profits are not paid out as dividends beyond a modest return of three per cent to shareholders; the society's rules require the rest to be spent for the benefit of the community.

G  The village is careful, however, not to claim too much. It is self-sufficient over a year, but not every hour. In calm, cloudy weeks in summer, the turbines produce little, and in dry spells the river slows. The village therefore remains connected to the national grid, drawing power when it needs it and sending power back when it has plenty. In 2020, a battery store was added, which holds spare energy from windy nights so that it can be used during quiet periods, and has raised the share of power the village uses directly from about half to nearly three quarters.

H  The effects have gone beyond electricity. The school, once threatened with closure, now has 80 pupils, as young families have moved in, attracted by the cheaper energy and the sense of purpose. The pub has a waiting list for its Friday evening meals. Neighbouring villages have asked for advice, and Calloway, now in her seventies, spends many weekends giving talks. Her advice is always the same. Start with one small project that people can see, such as a roof of solar panels on the village hall, and make sure that everyone has a voice. 'The technology is the easy part,' she says. 'It is the talking that takes the time.'  Even the pub has joined in, offering a discount on soup to anyone who arrives on a bicycle.
